sub: The Eucharistic liturgy of the Syro-Malabar Church: its meaning, its order and our part in it
sec: What the word means

“Qurbana” is the Syriac word for “offering”, from the root q-r-b, “to draw near, to offer”. In the Holy Qurbana the Church offers to the Father the one sacrifice of Christ, and Christ gives himself to us as the Bread of Life.

For the Syro-Malabar Church the Qurbana is not one devotion among others; it is the source and summit of the whole Christian life (Lumen Gentium 11). Every sacrament, every feast and every prayer leads to it and flows from it.
Its roots

The Syro-Malabar Church, heir to the faith preached by St Thomas the Apostle, celebrates in the East Syriac tradition, which it received through its ancient communion with the Church of the East. Its principal Eucharistic prayer is the Anaphora of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, one of the oldest anaphoras in the whole Church, attributed to the apostles of Edessa; the Church has also approved other ancient East Syriac anaphoras for particular days.

The restored Syro-Malabar Qurbana was approved by the Holy See in 1985 and revised later. The Synod of Bishops, with the approval of the Holy See, has laid down a uniform manner of celebration for the whole Church; obedience to the Synod and to the Holy See in liturgical matters is part of our communion.
How it unfolds

1. Preparation and beginning. The priest and ministers prepare at the altar. The celebration opens with “Glory to God in the highest” and the Lord's Prayer, with the response “Holy, holy, holy”. Psalms are prayed, and the hymn “Lakhu Mara” (“To you, O Lord”) praises Christ, the resurrection of our bodies and the saviour of our souls.

2. The Liturgy of the Word. The Trisagion is sung (“Holy God, holy Mighty One, holy Immortal One, have mercy on us”). The Scriptures are proclaimed: from the Law and the Prophets, from the Apostle, and finally the Gospel, received with lights and incense. The homily breaks open the Word. The Karozutha, a litany led by the deacon, gathers the prayers of the people.

3. The Liturgy of the Eucharist. The gifts are brought to the altar while the “Onitha d'Raze” (hymn of the mysteries) is sung; the Creed is professed; the peace is exchanged. In the Anaphora the priest prays the G'hanthas (prayers of inclination) and the Kusapas (prayers of humility); all sing the Sanctus; the priest recalls the Lord's Supper and pronounces his words; he calls down the Holy Spirit on the offering (Epiclesis). Then come the breaking of the bread and the signing of the Body with the Blood.

4. Communion and dismissal. After the Lord's Prayer and the invitation “The holy things are for the holy”, the faithful receive Holy Communion. Thanksgiving follows, and the final blessing (Huttama) sends the people out to live what they have received.
What the Church believes
The Qurbana makes present the one sacrifice of Christ on the Cross; it is not a new sacrifice (CCC 1366–1367).
Under the appearances of bread and wine Christ is truly, really and substantially present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity (CCC 1374–1376).
The Holy Spirit sanctifies the gifts and the people; East Syriac liturgy expresses this strongly in the Epiclesis (CCC 1353).
The Qurbana is celebrated in communion with the Pope, our Major Archbishop and our bishop, who are remembered in the prayers.
How to take part well

Come early, prepare in silence, and follow the movements of the liturgy: standing for the Gospel and the Anaphora, bowing, signing yourself. Answer and sing with the community; the Qurbana is the prayer of the whole people.
Keep the Eucharistic fast prescribed by the Church, receive with reverence, and remain for the thanksgiving. Bring your family; teach your children the responses and their meaning.
The sanctuary and its signs

A Syro-Malabar church is built as a picture of heaven and earth. The sanctuary (Madbaha), raised and veiled, stands for heaven; the nave (Hykala), where the people stand, stands for the world; between them lies the Qestroma, the threshold where heaven and earth meet. The veil is opened at the beginning of the celebration and closed after it: Christ has opened heaven to us.

Above the altar stands the Cross without the figure of the Crucified, often called the Mar Thoma Sliba: the Cross of the risen Lord, flowering at its ends, with the dove of the Holy Spirit. The altar faces east, towards the rising sun, the sign of Christ who will come again from the east (Matthew 24:27). The ancient East Syriac churches also had a Bema in the nave for the Liturgy of the Word.
Forms, vestments and gestures

The Syro-Malabar Qurbana has three forms: the Raza (the most solemn form, for great feasts), the solemn form, and the simple form used on most days. The Synod of Bishops has laid down a uniform mode of celebration for the whole Church: the priest faces the people during the Liturgy of the Word and the concluding rites, and faces the altar, with the people, towards the east during the Eucharistic Liturgy.

The priest wears the kuthina (white tunic), the urara (stole), the zande (cuffs), the zunara (girdle) and the phaina (the large outer vestment, like a cope). Incense, lights, bowing, kissing the altar and the sign of the Cross belong to the language of the Qurbana: they teach with the body what the words say.
Questions people ask
Why do we stand so much? Standing is the posture of the risen, of people ready to go; the East has always prayed standing, especially on Sundays.

Why the long prayers of humility (Kusapas)? Before the holy Mysteries the priest, and the whole people with him, confesses unworthiness and trust in mercy. Without humility no one can come near the altar.

Why is Communion received on the tongue? According to the norms of the Syro-Malabar Church, Holy Communion is normally received on the tongue, as a sign of reverence and of receiving a gift that we do not take for ourselves. Follow the norms of your eparchy.
How often may I receive? Catholics may receive every day; a second time on the same day only within a Qurbana in which they take part.
notes: Anyone conscious of grave sin must make a sacramental confession before receiving Holy Communion (CCC 1385).
Participation in the Holy Qurbana on Sundays and days of obligation is a grave duty (CCC 2180–2181).
Liturgical texts and the manner of celebration are determined by the Church's competent authority; no individual may change them on his own (Sacrosanctum Concilium 22; CCEO c. 657).
Disputes about the liturgy must never be carried on with disrespect to the Holy Eucharist, to the altar or to the Church's pastors.
Catholics receive Communion in Catholic celebrations, except in cases foreseen by Church law (CCC 1398–1401).
The Eucharistic fast before Holy Communion is laid down by the particular law of each Church sui iuris; follow the current norm of the Syro-Malabar Church (CCEO c. 713 §2).
refs: Lumen Gentium 11; Sacrosanctum Concilium 47–48; Orientalium Ecclesiarum 1–6

sub: How the Syro-Malabar Church walks through the whole mystery of Christ, season by season
sec: Why the Church keeps a year

Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever (Hebrews 13:8). Yet the Church does not celebrate his mystery all at once. In the course of one year she unfolds it step by step: the promise and birth of the Saviour, his manifestation, his fasting and Passion, his Resurrection, the gift of the Spirit, the mission of the apostles, the growth of the Church and the final fulfilment at his coming (CCC 1163–1171).

The liturgical year is therefore not a calendar of reminders. Each season makes present a part of the mystery, so that the faithful may enter it, be touched by it and be changed by it. The East Syriac Fathers loved to say that the Church walks with Christ through the year as Israel walked with God through the desert: feast by feast, fast by fast, towards the promised land.
Sunday, the heart of the year

Before there were seasons there was Sunday. From the day of the Resurrection the disciples gathered on the first day of the week to break bread (Acts 20:7). Sunday is the original feast, the weekly Easter, the foundation of the whole year (CCC 2174–2177).

In the Syro-Malabar tradition each Sunday has its own name within the season (for example, the Third Sunday of Annunciation) and its own set of four readings: two from the Old Testament (the Law and the Prophets), one from the Apostle and one from the Gospel. The Sunday Qurbana gathers the parish as one family around the altar.
How the dates are fixed

Two feasts anchor the year. The Nativity of the Lord is fixed on 25 December. Easter (the Qyamta) moves: it is kept on the Sunday after the first full moon following the spring equinox, according to the rule received from the Council of Nicaea (325).

Most of the year depends on Easter. Counting back: the Great Fast begins on the Monday seven weeks before Easter; the Fast of the Ninevites (Moonnu Nombu) falls a few weeks before the Great Fast; the season of Denha (Epiphany) is longer or shorter according to how early Easter comes. Counting forward: the Ascension on the fortieth day, Pentecost on the fiftieth, and the seasons of the Apostles and of Summer follow.

The year begins on the Sunday of Annunciation that falls between 27 November and 3 December, and ends with the last Sunday of the Dedication of the Church. The Syro-Malabar Church uses two sets of lectionary readings in alternate years; the official calendar published each year by the Major Archiepiscopal Curia tells which set is used.
The seasons of the Lord's coming and manifestation

1. Annunciation-Nativity (Subara). About four weeks of preparation, with the Sundays of the announcements: to Zechariah, to Mary, the birth of John, the revelation to Joseph. The Twenty-Five Days' Fast (1–25 December) belongs here. The Nativity of the Lord is celebrated on 25 December, often with a night Qurbana and, in many parishes, the ancient rite of the fire (Thee Uzhalichu) in which the faithful pass before a fire as a sign of Christ the Light.

2. Epiphany (Denha). Denha means “dawn” or “rising”. It begins on 6 January with the Baptism of the Lord in the Jordan, where the Father, the Son and the Spirit were revealed. In Kerala the night of Denha is kept with lights and the Pindiperunnal, the feast of the plantain stems decked with lamps. The Fridays of this season commemorate in turn John the Baptist, the apostles Peter and Paul, the four evangelists, St Stephen, the Greek Fathers, the Syrian Fathers, the patron of the parish and, on the last Friday, all the faithful departed.
The Great Fast, Holy Week and Easter

3. The Great Fast (Sawma Rabba). Fifty days of prayer, fasting and almsgiving. It begins on the Monday after Pethurta Sunday (the Sunday of “looking back”, of reconciliation before the fast); in many parishes ashes are blessed that day. The Wednesday of the fourth week marks mid-Lent; the fortieth Friday (Nalpathaam Velli) marks the end of the forty days of the Lord's fast.

Holy Week begins with the Saturday of Lazarus (in Kerala homes, Kozhukatta Saturday) and Hosanna Sunday (Oshana), with the procession of palms. On Pesaha Thursday the Church celebrates the Last Supper and the washing of the feet; families break the Pesaha appam at home with milk, remembering the Passover of the Lord. Good Friday is a day of mourning, fasting and the Way of the Cross; there is no Qurbana. Holy Saturday is a day of silence at the tomb.

4. Resurrection (Qyamta). Easter is the feast of feasts. The Sunday after Easter is the New Sunday (Puthunjayar), with the Gospel of St Thomas confessing “My Lord and my God”, a Sunday dear to the St Thomas Christians. The Ascension is kept on the fortieth day.
The seasons of the Church on mission

5. Apostles (Sliha). From Pentecost, when the Spirit came upon the apostles, the Church remembers their mission to the nations. The Dukrana of St Thomas, our Father in faith, is kept on 3 July; it is also kept as the day of the Syro-Malabar Church.

6. Summer (Qaita). The season of fruit: the Church, planted by the apostles, grows and bears fruit in holiness. The Assumption of Mary (15 August) usually falls in this season; many keep the devotional fast of the first fifteen days of August.

7. Elijah-Cross (Eliya-Sliba). Elijah, taken up to heaven, was expected to return before the Day of the Lord; the Cross is the sign of the Son of Man that will appear at his coming (Matthew 24:30). The Exaltation of the Holy Cross (14 September) gives the season its centre. The Eight Days' Fast before the Nativity of Mary (1–8 September) is widely kept.
8. Moses (Muse). Moses, who led the people to the edge of the promised land, turns our eyes to the end of the journey: judgment, the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.

9. Dedication of the Church (Qudash Edta). The last four Sundays celebrate the Church as the Bride of Christ, cleansed and adorned for the heavenly wedding. The year ends where history ends: in the Church gathered with her Lord.
Feasts, commemorations and fasts

The great feasts of the Lord are the Nativity, Denha, Easter, the Ascension and Pentecost. Other great days are the Dukrana of St Thomas (3 July), the Assumption of Mary (15 August), the Nativity of Mary (8 September), the Exaltation of the Cross (14 September) and the feasts of the saints of our own Church: St Alphonsa (28 July), St Kuriakose Elias Chavara (3 January), St Euphrasia (29 August) and St Mariam Thresia (8 June), among others.

The traditional fasts (Nombu) are the Twenty-Five Days' Fast before Christmas, the Three Days' Fast of the Ninevites, and the Great Fast. Devotional fasts kept by many are the fast of the first fifteen days of August and the Eight Days' Fast in September. Fasting in our tradition is never only a matter of food: it is joined to prayer, reconciliation and almsgiving.
Living the year at home

The liturgical year is meant to enter the home. Keep the crib and the star in Subara; light lamps at Denha; keep the Nombu as a family, choosing simpler meals and giving the savings to the poor; break the Pesaha appam on Pesaha Thursday; read the Gospel of the Sunday together on Saturday evening.

Name the season at family prayer (“This is the season of the Apostles”), pray for the intentions of the season, and let children know which saints are remembered. In this way the rhythm of the Church becomes the rhythm of the family, and the home becomes a little church.
notes: The obligation to take part in the Holy Qurbana on Sundays and days of obligation is grave; only a serious reason such as illness or the care of infants excuses (CCC 2180–2181).

The exact days of obligation and the rules of fasting and abstinence for the Syro-Malabar Church are laid down by its Synod of Bishops; follow the current particular law and the circulars of your eparchy, especially outside Kerala and abroad.
Fasting must never endanger health: the sick, pregnant and nursing mothers, the elderly and those doing heavy work should consult their pastor (cf. CCC 2043).

Customs such as Kozhukatta Saturday, the Pesaha appam, Pindiperunnal and the rite of the fire are traditions of the St Thomas Christians; they vary between regions and parishes. They are signs of faith, not substitutes for the liturgy.
On the number of seasons: some calendars count Elijah, Cross and Moses as a single season; the official Syro-Malabar calendar is the norm.
The Syro-Malabar Church has no liturgical colour code like the Roman Rite; do not judge a season by colour.
refs: Syro-Malabar Church, Liturgical Calendar (published yearly) and Thaksa of the Holy Qurbana

sub: Why we confess, how to examine our conscience, how to make a good confession, and what the Church asks of us
sec: Christ gave this sacrament

On the evening of Easter the risen Lord breathed on the apostles and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:22–23). Through the bishops and priests, their successors, Christ continues to forgive sins in the Church (CCC 1441–1445).

This sacrament has many names: conversion, penance, confession, forgiveness and reconciliation (CCC 1423–1424). In Kerala we usually say “Kumbasaram”. It is the sacrament of the prodigal son coming home and of the Father who runs to embrace him (Luke 15:20).
Why confess to a priest?

Only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7). But God chose to forgive through his Church: Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive and to retain, which they could not use without hearing the sins (CCC 1461–1462). The priest is not a judge who condemns but a minister of mercy who acts in the person of Christ, the Good Shepherd seeking the lost sheep (CCC 1465).

Sin is never purely private. It wounds the Body of Christ, the Church. So reconciliation with God is also reconciliation with the Church (CCC 1445, 1469). Hearing the words of absolution spoken aloud gives a certainty of forgiveness that our feelings alone cannot give.
Mortal and venial sin

Mortal sin destroys charity in the heart: it is a sin whose object is grave matter, committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857). Grave matter is specified by the Ten Commandments. Mortal sin, unless repented and forgiven, separates us from God for ever (CCC 1861).

Venial sin weakens charity but does not destroy it (CCC 1862–1863). Confessing everyday faults is strongly recommended: it helps us form our conscience, fight evil tendencies, let ourselves be healed by Christ and grow in the life of the Spirit (CCC 1458).
Examining the conscience

An honest examination is the first step. Some questions, following the Commandments: Do I pray daily? Have I denied my faith or been ashamed of it? Have I used God's name carelessly or sworn falsely? Have I missed the Holy Qurbana or Mass on Sundays and days of obligation without serious reason?

Have I honoured my parents and cared for them? Have I been unjust, violent or harsh at home, at work, with servants or employees? Have I harmed life: by anger, hatred, abortion, abuse of alcohol or drugs, reckless driving? Have I sinned against chastity in thought, word or deed, alone or with others, through pornography? Have I been faithful in marriage?

Have I stolen, cheated, taken bribes, failed to pay just wages or debts, wasted money while others are in need? Have I lied, gossiped, ruined another's good name, posted harmful things on social media? Have I been envious, greedy, proud, lazy in my duties? Have I neglected the poor?

Children and young people can ask more simply: Did I pray? Did I obey my parents and teachers? Did I tell lies, fight, use bad words, take what is not mine, cheat in exams, waste time on the phone, hurt anyone?
The three acts of the penitent

1. Contrition: sorrow of soul and hatred for the sin committed, with the resolution not to sin again. Perfect contrition comes from love of God; imperfect contrition (attrition) comes from fear of punishment or the ugliness of sin, and is sufficient for the sacrament (CCC 1451–1453).

2. Confession: telling the priest all mortal sins of which, after careful examination, we are conscious, with their kind and number, as far as we can (CCC 1456). Speak simply and honestly; there is no need for long stories or for naming other people.

3. Satisfaction: doing the penance the priest gives, to repair the harm and restore our habits as disciples of Christ (CCC 1459–1460). Where we have harmed others, we must also make it right: return what was taken, restore a damaged reputation, ask forgiveness.
How to make a good confession
Before: pray to the Holy Spirit for light; examine your conscience; awaken sorrow by looking at the crucifix and remembering God's love.

In the confessional: make the sign of the Cross; say how long it has been since your last confession and, if helpful, your state of life (married, student, priest or religious); confess your sins; listen to the priest's counsel and accept the penance; pray an act of contrition; receive absolution with faith. In the Eastern Churches the prayer of absolution often asks God to forgive the penitent; in the Latin Church the priest says “I absolve you”. Both are true and valid forms of the same sacrament.

A traditional act of contrition: O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended you, and I detest all my sins because of your just punishments, but most of all because they offend you, my God, who are all good and deserving of all my love. I firmly resolve, with the help of your grace, to sin no more and to avoid the near occasion of sin. Amen. (Any approved act of contrition may be used, such as the one taught in your parish catechism.)
After: thank God; do the penance soon; repair any harm done; avoid the occasions of sin; come back regularly, not only when burdened by grave sin.
What the sacrament gives

Reconciliation with God, by which grace is restored; reconciliation with the Church; remission of the eternal punishment due to mortal sin and, at least in part, of temporal punishment; peace and serenity of conscience and spiritual consolation; and an increase of strength for the Christian battle (CCC 1468–1470, 1496).

Many people find that the hardest step is the first one, the walk to the confessional. Beyond it is the joy of the Father: “this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found” (Luke 15:24).
Children, first confession and frequent confession

Children who have reached the age of discretion (around seven) are prepared for their first confession before their first Holy Communion (CCC 1457; c. 914). Parents should go with them and confess themselves; children learn most from what they see.

The saints recommend confessing regularly, for example monthly, and before the great feasts. Many parishes offer confession during the Twenty-Five Days' Fast and the Great Fast or Lent; make use of these times.
notes: Every Catholic who has reached the age of discretion must confess grave sins at least once a year (CCC 2042, 1457).

One who is conscious of mortal sin must not receive Holy Communion without first going to confession, except when there is a grave reason and no opportunity to confess; then an act of perfect contrition must be made, with the intention of confessing as soon as possible (CCC 1457, 1385).

Deliberately hiding a mortal sin in confession makes the confession invalid and adds the sin of sacrilege; the hidden sin and the sacrilege must be confessed. Forgetting a sin is not hiding it: the forgotten sin is forgiven and should be mentioned at the next confession.
The priest is bound by the absolute seal of confession: he may never reveal or use what he hears, under the most severe penalties (CCC 1467; Code of Canon Law c. 983; CCEO c. 733).
Absolution requires real contrition and the purpose of amendment; it cannot be given to one who refuses to give up a grave sin or to repair a grave injustice.

General absolution without individual confession is allowed only in grave necessity (danger of death, or very large numbers with no possibility of individual confession for a long time); grave sins must then be confessed individually as soon as possible (CCC 1483).
Some very grave sins carry penalties whose remission is reserved; if this concerns you, speak to a priest, who will explain the path of reconciliation.
refs: Code of Canon Law cc. 959–991; Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches cc. 718–736
